The New Testament. The New Testament is the second and shorter section of the Christian Bible, comprising twenty-seven texts written in Koine Greek during the first century. It centers on the life, ministry, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ and the early Christian movement he inspired. The New Testament includes the four Gospels—Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John—which narrate Jesus's life and teachings from different perspectives. It also contains the Acts of the Apostles, which chronicles the early church's expansion, Paul's letters to various communities, other epistles, and Revelation. Together with the Hebrew Bible, the Christian Old Testament, it constitutes Christian scripture and remains one of the most influential texts in Western civilization.

Matthew and Luke share similar material known as the Q source. Mark is the earliest Gospel, while John is philosophically distinctive. Jesus, the central figure, was a Jewish teacher and healer who was crucified by Roman authorities. His followers believed he was resurrected and understood him as the Messiah, or the Christ.

Paul, originally named Saul of Tarsus, was a Jewish Christian missionary who wrote the earliest Christian texts—his letters, dated around fifty to sixty-four CE. He argued that Christ's salvation was available to non-Jews, radically expanding Christianity's scope. The Gospels describe Jesus's teachings through parables, ethical instruction, and miracle accounts. The Sermon on the Mount, found in Matthew chapters five through seven, contains Jesus's most famous moral teachings. The Acts of the Apostles narrates the early church's formation, the apostles' missionary activities, and Christianity's expansion from Jerusalem into the Mediterranean world.

The epistles, or letters, address theological issues, ethical guidance, and pastoral concerns in early Christian communities. They are the earliest Christian theological writings and grapple with questions of faith, grace, and practice.
